papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Analysis of Microscopic Hyperspectral Images of HER2-Stained Breast Cancer Sections for Molecular Status Prediction.
papers.abstract: HER2 assessment in breast cancer relies on immunohistochemistry (IHC) with reflex in situ hybridization for equivocal cases, while conventional bright-field imaging provides limited quantitative optical information. We investigated microscopic hyperspectral imaging (HSI) of HER2-stained sections for slide-level molecular status prediction. HSI data from 43 cases (21 HER2-positive, 22 HER2-negative; 400-1000 nm, 128 bands) were acquired between January 2024 and August 2025. After calibration, optical-density conversion, tissue masking, and Savitzky-Golay smoothing, we developed SpectralMix-MIL, a weakly supervised multiple-instance learning model combining learnable spectral projection (K = 32) with attention pooling. On a patient-level 7:3 train/test split, SpectralMix-MIL achieved an AUROC of 0.923 and AUPRC of 0.910. Repeated stratified fivefold cross-validation yielded mean AUROC 0.904 ± 0.041 and AUPRC 0.892 ± 0.045, while leave-one-out cross-validation yielded AUROC 0.897. These findings support microscopic HSI for quantitative breast cancer molecular phenotyping, pending larger external validation.

papers.title: Rest-activity rhythm fragmentation, functional limitation, and mortality in adults with arthritis: A nationally representative cohort study.
papers.abstract: To characterize rest-activity rhythms in adults with arthritis, examine the role of functional limitation, and evaluate whether rhythm fragmentation is associated with mortality. We analyzed 7920 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) with at least 4 valid days of wrist accelerometry; arthritis status was available for 7904, including 2182 with arthritis. Nonparametric rest-activity rhythm features were evaluated using weighted linear and Cox models with primary-sampling-unit-clustered robust standard errors. Sensitivity analyses examined cohort selection and quadratic self-reported and device-estimated sleep duration. After demographic and clinical adjustment, arthritis was associated with higher intradaily variability (β = 0.063 SD, 95% CI 0.016-0.110) and lower most-active 10-hour (M10) activity (β = -0.030, 95% CI -0.051 to -0.009; both q = 0.028). Functional-limitation adjustment attenuated the intradaily variability difference (β = 0.005). Each 1-SD higher intradaily variability was associated with all-cause mortality after full adjustment (HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.10-1.26). Estimates were similar across alternative sleep-duration specifications and within participants with arthritis (HR 1.19, 95% CI 1.01-1.39). The estimated indirect effect through intradaily variability was near zero. Adults with arthritis had more fragmented rest-activity rhythms and lower peak daytime activity, with functional limitation accounting for most of the fragmentation difference. Higher fragmentation was associated with mortality, including within the arthritis subgroup, supporting further evaluation of this wearable-derived sleep-health and behavioral-rhythm phenotype in arthritis research.

papers.title: Interaction between unhealthy sleep pattern and obesity on cardiometabolic multimorbidity.
papers.abstract: Obesity and unhealthy sleep are established risk factors for cardiometabolic multimorbidity, but their joint effect remains unclear. This study aims to investigate their joint effect on cardiometabolic multimorbidity risk by analyzing data from 2 independent cohorts. We analyzed cross-sectional (Fuqing Cohort, N = 34,703) and prospective data (UK Biobank, N = 362,474; 12.3-year median follow-up, 3980 incident cardiometabolic multimorbidity cases). We defined unhealthy sleep (≥3 of 5 traits: late chronotype, sleep <7 or >8 h/day, frequent insomnia symptoms, self-reported snoring, frequent daytime sleepiness), cardiometabolic multimorbidity (≥2 of type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke), and obesity (general: BMI ≥25 kg/m²; central: waist circumference ≥80 cm in women, ≥94/90 cm in European/Asian men). The reference group had a sleep score <3 and no corresponding obesity. Logistic and Cox regressions evaluated associations and additive interaction was assessed. Unhealthy sleep and both obesity types independently increased cardiometabolic multimorbidity risk in both populations. The joint effect was stronger for unhealthy sleep combined with central obesity (FQC adjusted OR = 3.46; UKB adjusted HR = 2.55) than general overweight/obesity (FQC adjusted OR = 2.61; UKB adjusted HR = 2.46). Additive interaction showed stronger effect for unhealthy sleep with central versus general overweight/obesity in Europeans (adjusted RERI: 0.61 vs. 0.32). A similar additive interaction in Asians turned non-significant after covariate adjustment. Insomnia and central obesity showed a significant additive interaction in both cohorts. Unhealthy sleep and obesity jointly increase cardiometabolic multimorbidity risk, with central obesity having a stronger additive interaction than general overweight/obesity. Integrated public health strategies targeting sleep and weight are warranted.

papers.title: A geographic region analysis of sleep and obesity features in Chilean preschool-aged children.
papers.abstract: We evaluated the association between sleep and obesity stratified by geographic region in a large sample of preschool-aged children. Cross-sectional analysis of 278,382 Chilean preschoolers aged 3 to 6 years from a national school survey (April 2021-January 2022). Sociodemographic factors, anthropometry, and parent-reported sleep metrics (duration, midpoint) were analyzed. Adjusted generalized linear models with obesity-by-region interactions and multinomial logistic regression compared northern, central, and southern Chile. Main findings showed significant geographic variation. Compared to the central region, children in the southern region had longer nighttime sleep duration (B = 0.091 hours, 95% CI 0.079-0.104), earlier bedtimes (B = -0.097 hour, 95% CI -0.108 to -0.087), and earlier sleep midpoints (B = -0.052 hour, 95% CI -0.062 to -0.041). These children also had lower odds of sleep restriction (OR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.61-0.73) but higher odds of obesity (OR = 1.09, 95% CI 1.06-1.11). Compared with children without obesity, children with obesity showed shorter nighttime and total sleep duration and earlier wake-up times. The association between obesity and an earlier sleep midpoint varied by region (P for interaction = .035), whereas a later bedtime was observed only in the central region. Sleep characteristics in Chilean preschoolers vary by region and obesity status. Children in the southern regions have earlier and longer sleep compared to those in the central area, a pattern that may be related to geographic latitude. This more favorable sleep profile in the south persists despite a higher prevalence of obesity.

Current knowledge, key gaps, and opportunities for future research on high-impact, modifiable lifestyle behaviors to promote healthy aging in adults with cystic fibrosis in the era of modulator therapy.
papers.abstract: Aging in cystic fibrosis (CF), once a hopeful possibility, is now a celebrated reality for many and attributable to expert multidisciplinary care, persistent research efforts, and fervent advocacy. The median age of survival of people with CF (PWCF) increased dramatically with the advent of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapies, particularly elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in 2019. However, as PWCF live longer, healthy aging is susceptible to the compound impact of residual CFTR dysfunction, chronic inflammation, emerging comorbidities, complexities of chronic disease management, and psychosocial burdens. We define healthy aging as maintaining physical and mental health in adults so they can remain autonomous and independent as long as possible, while also adapting lifestyle habits to support well-being and improve overall quality of life. Lifestyle factors, such as stress, nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and treatment adherence, are known to impact health outcomes in the general population. Identifying, testing, and implementing behavioral interventions addressing these factors has the potential to augment medical advances in CF care. Although the aging population of PWCF is increasingly heterogeneous and shaped by unique individual ecosystems, lifestyle behaviors impact all patients and crosscut this diversity. As CF science continues to advance toward curative therapies, parallel CF-specific research advances on modifiable lifestyle behaviors may support healthier aging and improve health outcomes. This paper outlines the current state of knowledge, identifies critical gaps, and highlights key opportunities for future research targeting modifiable lifestyle behaviors to promote healthy aging, preserve functional independence, and improve quality of life in the growing population of adults with CF.

papers.title: Social Determinants of Sleep Health in Survivors of Childhood Cancer: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Survivors of childhood cancer frequently experience poor sleep quality, which affects behavioural, emotional, cognitive and physical health. Sleep health is multidimensional, encompassing regularity, satisfaction, alertness, timing, efficiency and duration, yet the influence of social, environmental and interpersonal factors on these dimensions remains poorly understood. This review examines sleep health dimensions among childhood cancer survivors and their associations with social determinants of health. A systematic review was completed in November 2025 using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO databases. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts, assessing links between social determinants and sleep outcomes. The risk of bias was evaluated using the ROBINS-E tool. Of 485 publications screened, 14 met the inclusion criteria. Most studies assessed sleep disturbances (n = 10), with fewer examining sleep duration (n = 5), alertness (n = 3) and sleep efficiency (n = 2). Social determinants, including race/ethnicity (n = 5), education (n = 6) and employment (n = 4), were associated with specific sleep dimensions; however, comprehensive analyses across the full spectrum of sleep remain limited. Social determinants influence several sleep dimensions among childhood cancer survivors, yet research rarely considers the multidimensional nature of sleep health. We propose a socio-ecological, multidimensional model to guide the development of targeted interventions and reduce sleep health disparities in this population.

papers.title: Cell-type- and subregion-specific basolateral amygdala inputs to ventral CA1-subiculum.
papers.abstract: The hippocampus is essential for learning and memory and interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions. Although the heterogeneity of intrinsic connectivity of hippocampal neurons is well established, the diversity of its extrahippocampal connectivity remains less understood. Such differential connectivity may contribute to functional diversity of hippocampal neurons in specific positions. Ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral subiculum (vSub) form strong reciprocal connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region critical for emotional and social regulation. Consequently, BLA-vCA1-vSub circuits have been implicated in anxiety-related and social behaviors. However, the functional connectivity from BLA to vCA1-vSub at the cellular and circuit levels is underexplored. To address this, we combined viral tracing with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted slice electrophysiology to examine BLA projections to vCA1-vSub in mice of either sex. We found that BLA inputs are not uniformly distributed along the transverse axis in vCA1-vSub. Instead, BLA selectively excites pyramidal neurons in distal vCA1-vSub while largely avoiding proximal vCA1 near CA2. BLA terminals strongly excited parvalbumin-expressing interneurons but only weakly recruited a small subset of somatostatin-expressing interneurons, generating robust disynaptic inhibitory synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons. Additionally, the same distal pyramidal neurons that receive BLA excitation also project back to the BLA. These findings reveal that BLA establishes cell-type- and subregion-specific excitatory connections within vCA1-vSub, highlighting a circuit architecture that may underlie functional heterogeneity in ventral hippocampal processing.Significance statement The hippocampus interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions, yet how long-range extrahippocampal inputs are organized across hippocampal subregions remains poorly understood. We examined projections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to the ventral hippocampus and found that BLA inputs selectively excite pyramidal neurons in distal ventral CA1 and ventral subiculum while largely avoiding proximal ventral CA1. BLA projections preferentially excite parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, provide disynaptic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons, and are reciprocally connected with the same pyramidal neurons in ventral CA1 and subiculum they excite. These findings reveal a highly selective connectivity pattern of amygdala-hippocampal circuits, providing a circuit framework for understanding how emotional information is routed through distinct ventral hippocampal pathways.

Association between triglyceride-glucose body mass index and future risk of arthritis in individuals with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome stages 0-3: A national prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome encompasses interrelated cardiovascular, renal and metabolic disorders. Arthritis is linked to CKM multimorbidity, but the association between triglyceride-glucose body mass index (TyG-BMI), a surrogate marker of insulin resistance and incident arthritis across the CKM spectrum remains unclear. We analyzed data from the CHARLS cohort, including 5018 participants aged ≥45 years with CKM stages 0 to 3. Analytical approaches included multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic splines, stratified and mediation analyses. Incident arthritis was defined by self-reported physician diagnosis, without confirmation via medical records. During follow-up, 2307 participants (45.97%) developed incident arthritis. Each one-standard-deviation increase in triglyceride-glucose body mass index (triglyceride-glucose body mass index) was associated with an 11% higher risk of arthritis (odds ratio [OR] = 1.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.04-1.19), with an approximately linear positive dose-response trend. The association appeared stronger in participants with sleep duration <7 hours (OR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.08-1.31) and those at CKM stage 1 (OR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.20-2.05). Exploratory mediation analyses suggested negative mediating roles of HDL-C and, marginally, BUN. Triglyceride-glucose body mass index exhibited an independent positive association with incident arthritis across CKM stages 0 to 3 and may serve as a practical indicator for early risk stratification.

papers.title: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma with METex14 mutation and high PD-L1: A case report.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC) is a rare and aggressive subtype of lung cancer, posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Cases of PSC harboring both MET exon 14 skipping (METex14) mutation and high PD-L1 expression are rarely documented, and reports detailing multimodal treatment involving surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy in such patients are even scarcer. A 54-year-old man presented with a persistent cough for over half a month. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed diminished breath sounds in the right upper lung. Initial bronchoscopic biopsy suggested inflammation, and computed tomography (CT)-guided lung biopsy showed atypical giant cells but was inconclusive. Following multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient underwent surgical resection. Postoperative pathology confirmed pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcomatoid carcinoma). Subsequent genetic testing identified a METex14 mutation with high PD-L1 expression (Tumor Proportion Score ≥ 50%). The final diagnosis was stage IIIB (T4N2M0) right PSC, MET-positive, PD-L1-positive. The initial treatment plan included 1 cycle of toripalimab (an anti-PD-1 antibody) combined with docetaxel and lobaplatin chemotherapy. This was subsequently adjusted to boretinib (a MET inhibitor) targeted therapy combined with docetaxel and lobaplatin chemotherapy. The patient achieved and maintained a partial response (PR) for over 6 months of follow-up. Symptoms including cough resolved, and his general condition remained good with satisfactory appetite and sleep. This case underscores the diagnostic difficulty of PSC, which is prone to misdiagnosis and exhibits rapid growth. Surgery may not be appropriate for unresectable stage IIIB PSC. Gene sequencing and PD-L1 testing are crucial as they expand therapeutic options for PSC patients. The optimal first-line therapy (targeted vs immunotherapy) for PSC with concurrent MET mutation and high PD-L1 expression remains undefined, warranting further exploration of combination strategies.

papers.title: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome associated with SLC16A2 c.1384G>A (p.Gly462Arg): A family case report with retrospective molecular diagnosis in a deceased sibling.
papers.abstract: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (monocarboxylate transporter 8 deficiency) is an X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in SLC16A2, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and a characteristic high-triiodothyronine (T3)/low-thyroxine (T4) thyroid profile. SLC16A2 c.1384G> A (p.Gly462Arg; NM_006517.5) was reported previously. We describe a Chinese family with the same variant, including retrospective molecular confirmation in a deceased maternal half brother. The proband was evaluated at 4.3 years for profound developmental delay. He could not sit, stand, or walk independently and had an intelligence quotient of 36, axial hypotonia with peripheral hypertonia, dystonia, muscle atrophy, joint contractures, and bilateral cryptorchidism. Thyroid testing showed elevated free triiodothyronine and total triiodothyronine, decreased free thyroxine and total thyroxine, and mildly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed delayed myelination, a thin corpus callosum, and widened frontal subarachnoid spaces. Whole-exome sequencing identified hemizygous SLC16A2 c.1384G> A (p.Gly462Arg); Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant in the proband and heterozygosity in his mother. The same hemizygous variant was detected in DNA from the archived neonatal dried blood spot of a maternal half brother who had severe developmental delay and died at 16 months. Thyroid tests, neuroimaging, and cause of death were not recorded for the deceased child. The proband received physical, occupational, and speech therapy and underwent bilateral orchiopexy. Triiodothyroacetic acid was not available at diagnosis. At the last documented follow-up at age 5 years, he remained unable to sit, stand, or walk independently. Clinical notes described improved head control, but no repeat standardized developmental score was available. Epileptiform electroencephalogram discharges persisted, but no clinical seizures were documented. This family provides additional clinical and segregation evidence for p.Gly462Arg. Testing an archived neonatal blood spot established the diagnosis in the deceased sibling and strengthened genetic counseling. SLC16A2 testing should be considered in boys with unexplained severe neurodevelopmental delay and a high-triiodothyronine/low-thyroxine pattern. Functional studies are still required to define the effect of p.Gly462Arg on monocarboxylate transporter 8 trafficking and thyroid hormone transport.

papers.title: Serum metabolic alterations associated with Chaihu-Longgu-Muli decoction in adolescents with insomnia: An exploratory untargeted metabolomics study.
papers.abstract: Adolescent insomnia is common and is frequently accompanied by anxiety and depressive symptoms. Chaihu-Longgu-Muli decoction (CLMD) is used in traditional Chinese medicine prescriptions for insomnia; however, the biological changes associated with CLMD treatment in adolescents remain poorly characterized. This exploratory study investigated clinical symptom changes and corresponding serum metabolomic alterations associated with CLMD treatment in adolescents with chronic insomnia. Adolescents with chronic insomnia received either CLMD or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) according to the predefined treatment-allocation procedure. A healthy control group was included for baseline metabolic comparison. Sleep quality and emotional symptoms were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS). Fasting serum samples collected before and after the intervention underwent untargeted metabolomic profiling using ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry. Candidate differential metabolites were identified using multivariate analysis together with a variable importance in projection score > 1.0 and nominal P < .05, followed by pathway enrichment analysis. Given the exploratory nature of the study, metabolomic findings were considered hypothesis-generating. Thirty adolescents were included in each intervention group, with an additional 10 healthy controls. Both CLMD and CBT groups showed improvements in PSQI, SAS, and SDS measures after treatment (all P < .05). Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified differences between adolescents with insomnia and healthy controls. Among the exploratory candidate metabolites, sphinganine and 3-indoleacetonitrile were higher in adolescents with insomnia, whereas ethylmethylacetic acid, choline, L-lysine 1,6-lactam, (R)-2-O-sulfolactate, cis-aconitic acid, and sorbitol were lower (all P < .05). Following CLMD treatment, these metabolites shifted toward levels observed in healthy controls. Exploratory pathway analysis implicated the intestinal immune network for IgA production, sphingolipid signaling, PPAR signaling, and bile secretion. CLMD treatment was associated with improvements in insomnia-related symptoms and concurrent changes in serum metabolic profiles in adolescents with chronic insomnia. The identified metabolites and pathways represent preliminary biological signals rather than validated biomarkers or established mechanisms. Larger studies with targeted quantitative metabolomics and independent validation are needed.

papers.title: Effects of Tai Chi combined with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on sleep and emotional outcomes in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Sleep problems are common in older adults and are frequently accompanied by emotional symptoms, including depression, anxiety, and stress. Tai Chi and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) have both been applied as non-pharmacological interventions for sleep and mood regulation. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of their combined use remains limited. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Scopus from inception to December 16, 2025, to identify randomized controlled trials. The search strategy combined terms related to Tai Chi, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, and randomized controlled trials. Reference lists of relevant articles were also screened to identify additional eligible studies. Pooled mean differences with 95% confidence intervals were generated using RevMan 5.4, with risk of bias and certainty assessed through established tools including GRADE. Three trials encompassing 211 older adults qualified for analysis. Combined Tai Chi and rTMS was associated with a significant reduction in sleep severity compared with control interventions (SMD = -0.51; 95% CI: -0.90 to -0.12; P = .01; I2 = 43%). Evidence for other sleep-related outcomes and for depression, anxiety, and stress was inconclusive. The available evidence suggests that the combination of Tai Chi and rTMS may improve overall sleep severity; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of trials and sensitivity to individual studies. Evidence for specific sleep parameters and emotional outcomes remains inconclusive. Further well-designed randomized trials are needed to clarify the potential role of this combined intervention in sleep and mood regulation.

papers.title: Global research landscape and emerging frontiers in primary insomnia treatment (2005-2025): A bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate the current state of research on primary insomnia, focusing on key trends and global hotspots. The Web of Science Core Collection database was used as the primary source for identifying peer-reviewed studies on therapeutic approaches to primary insomnia between 2005 and 2025. CiteSpace analytical tools were employed to examine bibliometric indicators, including temporal publication trends, international collaboration networks, institutional productivity rankings, high-impact journals, influential researchers, conceptual co-citation clusters, and keyword evolution patterns. A systematic search identified 2826 relevant publications published over the 2-decade period from 2005 to 2025. Our analysis revealed the journals, countries, institutions, and authors with the highest output in primary insomnia treatment. The United States and the University of California System were the most productive country and institution, respectively. The journal Sleep dominated scholarly productivity and citation metrics. The journal Sleep emerged as a leading scholarly outlet in somnology research, consistently ranking among the most frequently cited journals. The analyzed publications involved 15,657 distinct researchers; Charles M. Morin and Daniel J. Buysse were the most frequently co-cited authors, followed by Célyne H. Bastien, Maurice M. Ohayon, Dieter Riemann, and Jack D. Edinger. Research on primary insomnia treatment has evolved from behavioral therapies to cognitive behavioral therapy and precision medicine. Current hotspots focus on digital therapeutics, neuromodulatory drugs, and comorbid mechanisms, while future advancements are expected to leverage multi-omics and artificial intelligence for personalized interventions. By employing advanced scientometric methods, this study systematically maps conceptual developments and intellectual progress in primary insomnia through rigorous literature mining and knowledge visualization. It identifies emerging trends and key challenges in somnology, offering valuable insights for researchers developing therapeutic strategies. The findings provide a clear overview of research evolution over the past 2 decades, highlighting current focuses and future directions. However, this analysis reflects publication trends within the Web of Science Core Collection only and does not assess clinical efficacy or treatment priorities. Notably, 2025 data include publications only up to March 7, representing an incomplete year. Overall, this work provides a concise knowledge base to inform future research in primary insomnia.

papers.title: Mental health trajectories before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic among patients attending a psychosomatic internal medicine clinic in Japan: A retrospective quantitative study.
papers.abstract: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has exacerbated anxiety and depression globally, particularly among individuals with mental health conditions and chronic illnesses. However, the extent to which these mental health effects have persisted following the pandemic remains unclear. This study examined changes in mental health before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic among first-time patients attending a psychosomatic internal medicine clinic in Japan. The legal reclassification of COVID-19 to "Class5" status under Japan's Infectious Diseases Control Law, which took effect on May 8 2023, serves as the benchmark marking the beginning of the post-pandemic era, designated as the beginning of the post-pandemic period. The General Health Questionnaire (GHQ)-30, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) were used to assess general mental health, state and trait anxiety, and depressive symptoms, respectively. Participants were classified into pre-pandemic (n = 87), during-pandemic (n = 322), and post-pandemic (< 1 year: n = 75 and 1-2 years: n = 68) groups. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare mental health outcomes across the study periods. A total of 552 participants completed the survey (237 men and 315 women; mean age: 44.57 ± 19.56 years). Within 1 year after the pandemic, GHQ total mean scores, sleep disturbance, anxiety and dysphoria, and CES-D mean scores were significantly higher than those in the pre-pandemic group (GHQ total: 16.32 vs 13.57, P = .015; sleep disturbance: 3.70 vs 2.65, P < .001; anxiety and dysphoria: 3.14 vs 2.35, P = .016; CES-D: 26.53 vs 21.39, P = .005). Sleep disturbance scores were also significantly higher within 1 year after the pandemic than during the pandemic (3.70 vs 3.19, P = .015) but were significantly lower in the 1 to 2 years post-pandemic group than in the within-one-year post-pandemic group (2.65 vs 3.70, P = .022). These findings suggest that symptoms of anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance persisted during the early post-pandemic period but gradually improved over time. Particularly, sleep disturbance remained one of the most persistent mental health concerns, highlighting the importance of continued attention to the mental health of patients with psychosomatic disorders following the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Associations of Artificial Light at Night with Multi-Organ Biological Aging: Epidemiological Evidence from a Middle-Aged and Elderly Urban Population.
papers.abstract: Organ systems age asynchronously, and disruptions of circadian timing may drive coordinated organ-specific decline. Artificial light at night (ALAN) is a pervasive perturbation that may contribute to socioeconomic gradients in biological aging. Yet its contribution to systemic, multi-organ aging remains poorly characterized. Long-term ALAN exposure (2006-2010) for 37,323 urban UK Biobank participants was evaluated from a cross-calibrated, 500 m NPP-VIIRS-like nighttime-light dataset. Organ-specific biological aging across 11 systems was quantified using organ-enriched plasma proteins and a composite proteomic age gap. Associations of ALAN with organ-specific age gaps were estimated using multivariable linear regression through modeling. Dose-response relationships were evaluated using natural cubic splines with three degrees of freedom. Subgroup analyses by age, sex, socioeconomic status (SES), societal aging, and urbanization level were conducted. Higher ALAN exposure was associated with accelerated aging in several organ systems. In categorical analyses, the strongest association was observed for the brain (β=0.21, 95% CI: 0.08-0.33), followed by the intestine (high vs. low: β=0.15, 95% CI: 0.04-0.26) and pancreas (β=0.09, 95% CI: 0.01-0.18). Dose-response revealed significant monotonic increases, particularly for brain and pancreas aging. Lung, intestine, and adipose aging were stronger among males, and the effect modification by SES was limited to kidney aging (all FDR -adjusted P for interaction<0.05). Long-term ALAN exposure is associated with accelerated proteomic aging in specific organ systems, most consistently the brain, pancreas, and intestine. These findings identify ALAN as a modifiable environmental factor that warrants further investigation in longitudinal and intervention studies to determine whether reducing ALAN exposure can promote healthy aging and reduce socially patterned differences in aging vulnerability.

papers.title: Impact of Combined Chronic Stress and REM Sleep Deprivation on Memory Function and Hippocampal BDNF Protein Content in Wistar Rats.
papers.abstract: The concurrent impact of chronic psychological stress and sleep disruption on systemic adaptation and hippocampal cytoarchitecture remains poorly understood. This study investigated the neurobiological threshold of compounded stress by exposing male Wistar rats to combined Chronic Unpredictable Mild Stress (CUMS) and Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Deprivation (RSD), specifically chosen over total sleep deprivation due to the unique role of REM sleep in emotional regulation and spatial memory consolidation over 21 days. We evaluated body weight loss, sensorimotor function Open Field Test (OFT), declarative memory Novel Object Recognition (NOR), serum corticosterone, hippocampal malondialdehyde (MDA), and Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF). Results revealed that the combined stress paradigm precipitated significant body weight loss while preserving basal locomotor activity. In contrast to motor preservation, spatial recognition memory was significantly impaired. Biochemically, serum corticosterone and hippocampal MDA levels did not show statistically significant differences across groups. Crucially, while isolated CUMS significantly suppressed hippocampal BDNF protein content and RSD exhibited a similar trend of reduction, the combined paradigm triggered a compensatory neurotrophic rebound, returning BDNF to control baseline levels. However, the localized BDNF rebound did not translate to recovery cognitive performance. These findings suggest a phenomenon of neurobiological dissociation under compounded stress exposure. The organism experiences significant body weight loss and declarative memory impairment, while simultaneously initiating a localized, yet functionally ineffective, compensatory BDNF response in the hippocampus.

papers.title: Sleep complaints in alexithymia reflect non-specific negative affectivity.
papers.abstract: Alexithymia is the inability to identify and describe emotions, associated with an increased risk of somatic and psychiatric disease. Alexithymia is also characterized by reduced subjective sleep quality. However, it is not well-known if this reduction in sleep quality reflects physiological changes in sleep, a specific alteration in perceived sleep quality not captured by objective metrics, or a non-specific spillover of the negative affective style which characterizes alexithymia. In BSETS, a large (N = 228) in-home EEG study of naturalistic sleep, we found that alexithymia symptoms are associated with worse habitual (AIS) and current (GSQS) subjective sleep quality (βAIS = 0.207, pAIS = 0.002, βGSQS = 0.203, pGSQS = 0.002). However, we observed no significant association between alexithymia and EEG-based sleep efficiency (β = -0.017, p = 0.791). The association with subjective sleep quality was almost completely attenuated when controlling for either depressive symptoms (PHQ-9, βAIS = 0.001, pAIS = 0.982, βGSQS = 0.044, pGSQS = 0.486) or trait neuroticism (ZKPQ, BFI-44, βAIS = 0.057, pAIS = 0.442, βGSQS = 0.048, pGSQS = 0.514). A possible exception is the Difficulty Identifying Feelings alexithymia dimension, reflecting complaints about the labeling of interoceptive experiences, which was associated with lower subjective sleep quality even after covariate control. This pattern of findings suggests that alexithymia is characterized only by alterations of subjective sleep quality, and even these reflect a non-specific increase in negative affect which influences self-reports of sleep quality, rather than a specific reduction in perceived sleep quality itself.

papers.title: Infusion timing and outcomes after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation across graft sources.
papers.abstract: Circadian regulation can shape immune activation and has been linked to outcomes after immunotherapy and cellular therapies. In allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT), whether graft infusion time influences graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), non-relapse mortality (NRM), or hematopoietic recovery remains uncertain, and prior clinical studies have largely focused on single graft sources. To determine whether clock time of graft infusion is associated with transplant outcomes after allo-HCT and whether these associations differ among bone marrow transplantation (BMT), peripheral blood stem cell transplantation (PBSCT), and cord blood transplantation (CBT). We retrospectively analyzed 1,714 consecutive patients aged 16 years or older who underwent first allo-HCT at our institution from 2004 through 2025. Patients were stratified by graft source. Infusion time was defined as the recorded graft-product release time from the transfusion service to the transplant ward. Based on the institutional infusion-time distribution, infusions before 16:00 were classified as Early and those at or after 16:00 as Late. Propensity score matching was performed separately within each graft source, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used as a complementary analysis. The primary endpoint was 5-year NRM. Secondary endpoints included overall survival, progression-free survival, relapse, neutrophil and platelet engraftment, and acute GVHD. The cohort included 1,008 BMT, 478 PBSCT, and 228 CBT recipients. Propensity score matching generated 242, 172, and 63 Early-Late pairs, respectively. Five-year NRM for Early vs. Late infusion was 18.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 13.1-23.1) vs. 19.4% (95% CI, 14.2-24.4) after BMT (P = 0.78), 20.7% (95% CI, 13.6-27.1) vs. 26.4% (95% CI, 18.5-33.5) after PBSCT (P = 0.23), and 16.4% (95% CI, 5.6-26.1) vs. 17.8% (95% CI, 6.8-27.5) after CBT (P = 0.88). Fifty-day neutrophil engraftment was similar after BMT (95.5% [95% CI, 92.6-97.2] vs. 94.8% [95% CI, 91.8-96.8]; P = 0.62), PBSCT (97.1% [95% CI, 94.1-98.6] vs. 96.2% [95% CI, 92.8-98.0]; P = 0.47), and CBT (81.6% [95% CI, 70.0-88.7] vs. 79.7% [95% CI, 67.6-87.2]; P = 0.75). The 100-day cumulative incidence of grade II-IV acute GVHD also did not differ significantly after BMT (37.6% [95% CI, 31.2-43.4] vs. 43.3% [95% CI, 36.8-49.2]; P = 0.20), PBSCT (32.5% [95% CI, 25.2-39.1] vs. 30.2% [95% CI, 23.0-36.7]; P = 0.65), or CBT (35.9% [95% CI, 23.1-46.6] vs. 33.7% [95% CI, 20.9-44.3]; P = 0.79). IPTW analyses showed no significant association between Late infusion and NRM, survival, relapse, engraftment, or acute GVHD across the three graft sources. In this graft source-stratified cohort, earlier infusion across the 16:00 threshold was not associated with improved outcomes. These findings do not support routinely changing graft handling or infusion workflows solely to achieve earlier infusion within the afternoon range. The potential benefit of morning infusion remains to be determined.
