papers.title: Asthma and Impaired Sleep: Identifying Treatable Traits in the SCAPIS Study.
papers.abstract: This study compared sleep quality and insomnia symptoms in individuals with and without asthma and identified potentially treatable traits that could be used to improve sleep in asthma. This cross-sectional analysis included 28,828 participants (aged 50-64). Post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) were measured. Questionnaires assessed physician-diagnosed asthma, asthma-related symptoms, exacerbations, allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS), nocturnal breathing disorders and reflux (snoring, sleep apnea, nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux [nGER]), and sleep quality. Insomnia symptoms included difficulties initiating sleep (DIS), difficulties maintaining sleep (DMS), and early morning awakening (EMA). Current asthma was associated with impaired sleep quality (OR=1.56; [95% CI:] 1.39-1.75), DIS (1.59; [1.40-1.81]), DMS (1.36; [1.22-1.51]), EMA (1.31; [1.16-1.48]), and any insomnia symptom (1.38; [1.25-1.52]). Among individuals with asthma, allergic rhinitis was linked to impaired sleep quality (1.28; [1.01-1.62]), while CRS, asthma symptoms, exacerbations, snoring, sleep apnea and nGER were associated with impaired sleep quality and insomnia symptoms. Those with uncontrolled asthma, CRS, or nocturnal breathing disorders and reflux had higher odds of impaired sleep quality and any insomnia symptom, with the strongest associations in those with all three conditions (5.68; [3.47-9.29] and 3.63; [2.26-5.85], respectively). Asthma is associated with impaired sleep quality and insomnia symptoms in middle-aged adults. Our study also indicates that in asthma, impaired sleep quality and insomnia symptoms are linked to three potentially treatable traits, namely lack of asthma control, upper airway disorders, and nocturnal breathing disorders and reflux.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbance and Associated Factors in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Patients Receiving HAIC Combined with Immunotherapy and Targeted Therapy: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: This study assessed the prevalence of sleep disturbance and associated factors in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) receiving hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) combined with targeted therapy and immunotherapy. A cross-sectional survey enrolled 230 patients undergoing HAIC combined with targeted therapy and immunotherapy at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (July-November 2025). Sleep, psychological distress, pain, appetite, and quality of life were assessed using the PSQI, HADS, NRS, VAS, and EORTC QLQ-C30, respectively, along with prior HAIC cycles. Logistic regression identified factors associated with sleep disturbance. The prevalence of sleep disturbance (PSQI > 5) was 72.6% (167/230). Univariate analysis identified a greater number of prior HAIC cycles, higher levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, and lower quality of life and appetite as significant factors. In multivariate analysis, four factors remained independently associated with sleep disturbance: prior HAIC cycles (OR = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.25-2.20, P < 0.001), anxiety symptoms (OR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.12-1.44, P < 0.001), depressive symptoms (OR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.03-1.47, P = 0.021), and appetite sensations (OR = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.91-0.96, P < 0.001), which showed an inverse association with sleep disturbance. The model showed an apparent area under the ROC curve of 0.92 (95% CI 0.87-0.96), with an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.91 after bootstrap resampling. Sleep disturbance was highly prevalent and was independently associated with cumulative treatment burden, psychological distress and impaired appetite. These cross-sectional findings support routine sleep screening together with psychological and nutritional assessment in this population; whether modifying these factors improves sleep quality requires prospective interventional studies.

papers.title: From hypoxia to thrombosis: a hypothesis-driven framework for pulmonary embolism risk in deep underground environments.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the most severe manifestations of venous thromboembolism, yet current diagnostic and preventive frameworks have largely been developed in ground-based clinical settings. Deep underground environments represent complex occupational exposure systems characterized by relative hypoxia or oxygen fluctuation, normobaric to mildly hyperbaric pressure, high humidity and heat, airborne particulates, radon accumulation, restricted ventilation, limited mobility, circadian disruption, and enclosed psychosocial stress. These factors may interact dynamically with oxygen sensing, cardiopulmonary compensation, venous return, endothelial function, and coagulation-inflammation pathways. However, the relationship between deep underground exposure, thrombogenesis, PE recognition, and prevention remains insufficiently conceptualized. Direct epidemiological evidence linking deep-underground occupational exposure to incident venous thromboembolism or PE remains scarce, and existing PE prediction tools have not been specifically validated in deep-underground occupational populations. Therefore, this review does not assume that underground exposure independently increases PE incidence or that established clinical tools are inadequate. Instead, we develop a hypothesis-driven framework to examine whether exposure-related factors-including oxygen fluctuation, heat and dehydration, restricted mobility, altered hemodynamics, and inflammatory stress-could modify thrombotic susceptibility, symptom interpretation, or the operational performance of conventional PE pathways. We summarize the environmental and physiological stressors relevant to PE, examine how they may amplify Virchow's triad, and discuss research questions concerning symptom recognition, anticoagulation, reperfusion decision-making, preventive interventions, and the staged development of dynamic risk warning models. This review aims to provide a conceptual foundation for future surveillance, prevention, and clinical research on PE in deep underground occupational populations.

papers.title: Ursolic acid as a multi-target therapeutic candidate in type 2 diabetes mellitus: a mechanistic and translational review.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is interconnected disturbances in insulin signaling, pancreatic β-cell function, redox and inflammatory homeostasis, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and signaling mediated by advanced glycation end-product (AGE) and their receptors (RAGE). Although available antidiabetic therapies provide substantial clinical benefit, progressive β-cell dysfunction, and diabetes-associated tissue injury remain important clinical challenges. Ursolic acid (UA), a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid, has demonstrated broad preclinical metabolic and organ-protective effects, but the supporting evidence remains fragmented across individual pathways and experimental models. This review provides as updated, T2DM focussed in vitro, animal and limited human evidence, integrating UA-specific findings across insulin receptor/PTP1B signaling, β-cell preservation, redox regulation, inflammation, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis and AGE-RAGE-associated injury. A key contribution is to stratify the mechanistic evidence rather than treating all pathway associations as equivalent, distinguishing direct or intervention-supported findings from expression-level associations, computational predictions and effects that may occur secondarily to improvements in glycaemia, insulin sensitivity, adiposity or oxidative stress. The review focus is comparatively stronger for the insulin-sensitising, lipid-regulatory, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of UA, whereas direct AGE-RAGE modulation, circadian regulation and some pathway specific β-cell mechanisms remain preliminary. The translational development of UA is constrained by poor aqueous solubility, low oral bioavailability, uncertain dose exposure relationships, limited dose standardisation, insufficient long-term safety data, and lack of robust clinical validation in patients with T2DM. UA represents a multi-target preclinical candidate, rather than a clinically established antidiabetic therapy. Future research should prioritise pathway-specific validation, standardized diabetes-relevant models, pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic correlation, controlled clinical studies, and long-term safety assessment.
papers.journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders

papers.title: Intervention on modifiable lifestyle and physiological factors via variational autoencoder reveals changes in functional connectivity-mediated risk for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains without effective treatment, largely due to the fact that clinical symptoms emerge only after decades of silent pathological progression. It is urgently needed to identify modifiable risk factors in earlier life stages, when preventive interventions may still be effective. Functional connectivity (FC) has emerged as a promising neuromarker for both neurodegenerative processes and behavioral traits, making it a potential bridge between early-life health profiles and late-life AD risk. In this work, we introduce a novel integrative framework, called InterventionVAE, that models how early-life lifestyle and physiological factors influence AD risk through their impact on brain FC. Our approach combines a modified variational autoencoder (VAE) that simulates FC changes under interventions with a predictive model that estimates AD risk based on FC patterns. This design enables training of the generative and predictive components under different datasets and populations, with FC acting as the bridge between early-life modifiable factors and late-life disease risk. Applying InterventionVAE to data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), UK Biobank (UKB), and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we validate its ability to capture known risk factors, such as age and polygenic risk score, on FC-mediated AD risk. We also identify earlier-life modifiable factors including tobacco use, sleep quality, physical activity, and weight/BMI that significantly influence AD risk. Notably, we observe a U-shaped relationship between blood pressure and AD risk, and highlight the brain visual and somatomotor networks as key mediators of risk through FC. Our approach provides a powerful tool for investigating the effect pathways linking early-life interventions to neurodegenerative outcomes, with broad applicability to other brain-related disorders.

papers.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
papers.abstract: The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

papers.title: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline and drug-induced encephalopathy secondary to teprotumumab for thyroid eye disease: a case report and narrative literature review.
papers.abstract: Teprotumumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R), is an approved targeted therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is an extremely rare but potentially severe central nervous system adverse event, with only three cases reported globally to date. We report the first Han-Chinese patient with Graves' disease and associated TED complicated by teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy, together with a narrative review of all published cases, to raise clinicians' awareness and improve early recognition and management of this rare complication. A 56-year-old Chinese man with Graves' disease and TED developed acute progressive apathy and encephalopathy characterised by multidomain cognitive and behavioral dysfunction 20 days after the third teprotumumab infusion, with an admission MMSE score of 15. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening were unremarkable. Prolonged video-electroencephalography(VEEG) demonstrated intermittent diffuse bilateral slow-wave activity, and widespread interictal epileptiform discharges without electrographic or clinical seizures. Systematic workup excluded infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and psychiatric encephalopathy. Treatment-emergent hyperglycemia was confirmed as a secondary aggravating factor rather than the primary cause. The patient achieved prominent neurological recovery after individualized treapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) and symptomatic management, with a Naranjo score of 6 indicating probable drug-related encephalopathy. Synthesis of all three previously published teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy cases demonstrates that neurological toxicity can develop as early as the third infusion cycle. These cases present consistent neuroimaging features with variable CSF profiles, and thyroid autoantibody elevation predominantly reflects pre-existing Graves' disease-related autoimmune background instead of directly mediating neurotoxicity. TPE generally facilitates neurological recovery but may be complicated by procedural hypersensitivity and fluctuating therapeutic responses. Notably, interictal epileptiform discharges on VEEG represent a newly identified neurophysiological manifestation of this rare adverse event. A three-hit interacting pathogenic hypothesis is proposed: impaired IGF-1R-dependent neurotrophic signalling serves as the core injury mechanism, while underlying thyroid autoimmunity and treatment-related metabolic disturbance act as susceptibility-modifying factors. This case expands the ethnic and clinical spectrum of teprotumumab-related encephalopathy. Diffuse interictal epileptiform discharges without ictal changes reflect reactive cortical hyperexcitability secondary to acute encephalopathy. Metabolic disturbance merely exacerbated neurological impairment. Limitations include single-case constraints, simultaneous multi-intervention therapy, and lack of direct intracranial mechanistic evidence. Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is a rare but serious adverse event. Close neurological surveillance and are essential during medication. Accumulated cases are needed to establish unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.

papers.title: AI Health Coach Prototype and Personalized Pathophysiological Hypotheses Based on an N-of-1 Big Data Study of Non-specific Musculoskeletal Chronic Pain.
papers.abstract: Background Modern healthcare is shifting towards predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory medicine. While machine learning (ML) forecasting has seen success in episodic conditions, translating these results to non-specific musculoskeletal chronic pain is challenging due to the logistical barriers of collecting high-density, continuous longitudinal data across large cohorts. Therefore, this study leverages a high-density n-of-1 dataset to (i) generate personalized data-driven hypotheses about symptom-stressor associations and pathophysiology, and (ii) explore the feasibility of a prospective AI prediction tool. Methods A longitudinal n-of-1 observational study was conducted on a single adult male with mechanically exacerbated non-specific musculoskeletal chronic pain. Over 10 years (utilizing a 28-month core analysis window), continuous subjective daily pain logging was combined with high-resolution physiological monitoring via a commercial wearable ecosystem. Feature engineering utilized the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) framework to quantify physiological stressors across three pain regions (face, knee, and arm). Data were analyzed using Pearson correlations, and random forest classifiers were trained to generate a daily, actionable AI-generated traffic light flare warning system. Results Both correlation analyses and single-stressor random forest models revealed that stressors applying direct mechanical load to a specific region (e.g., computer use for face pain, step count for knee pain) were most strongly associated with symptom flares, outperforming systemic variables like sleep or mood. In the held-out test set, the AI coach prototype achieved receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.93 (face), 0.78 (knee), and 0.82 (arm) between clearly high and low pain days and correctly flagged each region's single most severe flare with a red or orange warning before its peak. Since only one such flare occurred per region, this should be read as an illustrative result rather than an estimate of general reliability; a fuller, more mixed picture across all flare events is reported in Results. Furthermore, evaluation on a subsequent follow-up dataset held out during previous training and tuning decisions showed decreased alert performance, reflecting real-world deployment complexities or genuine instability in the learned stressor-pain relationships. Regardless, prediction probabilities still rose before flares. Finally, counterfactual analysis of an ergonomic intervention through AI predictions led to results consistent with, but not proof of, ergonomics-related pain reduction. Conclusions This proof-of-concept illustrates how an automated n-of-1 pipeline can serve a dual function. First, combining linear correlation with non-linear ML on ACWR-engineered features, this study identifies associations between regional mechanical load and pain symptoms that are consistent with, but do not establish, a load-related pain mechanism such as bottom-up central sensitization, and points toward the envelope of function as a candidate therapeutic framework. Second, it illustrates the potential to translate these associations into a foundational just-in-time adaptive intervention system, empowering patients to proactively manage daily mechanical loads. Future integration of objective biological markers may further transition such tools from associative forecasting to true causal understanding.

papers.title: Overcoming subject variability in P300 decoding based on quantification by deep learning.
papers.abstract: Binary P300 decoding is a cornerstone of P300-based brain-computer interfaces, enabling applications such as assistive communication, neurorehabilitation, and cognitive monitoring. However, substantial subject variability in EEG patterns poses a major challenge to the development of generalized P300 decoders. To address this problem, this study proposes SQ_EMoE, a subject-variability-aware enhanced Mixture-of-Experts framework that uses the confidence produced by a deep subject-identification network as a practical proxy for trial-level subject distinctiveness. High-confidence trials are routed to subject-specific experts, whereas uncertain trials are redirected to a pooled general expert, allowing the framework to dynamically balance subject-specific specialization and cross-subject generalization. Latent subject representations are further visualized to qualitatively examine subject separability and its relationship with routing behavior. Experiments on eight random subjects from each of two public P300 datasets yielded mean ROC-AUC values of approximately 0.86 on BNCI Horizon 2020 and 0.89 on P300-LINI, outperforming pooled EEGNet and architecture-matched pooled P300MCNN baselines. Ablation experiments further demonstrated the contribution of confidence-controlled fallback to the general expert. To evaluate scalability, the framework was additionally tested on all 22 subjects of P300-LINI. With the original subject-identification network, SQ_EMoE achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.8518; after strengthening the subject representation and identification network, performance increased to 0.8760, exceeding the pooled P300MCNN baseline (0.8482) and slightly surpassing the oracle routing or within-subject decoding (0.8744). Leave-one-subject-out experiments further showed that the under-realized SQ_EMoE conservatively redirects most completely unseen-subject trials to the general expert when reliable subject-specific routing is unavailable. These results demonstrate that effective modeling of subject variability, together with adaptive integration of shared and subject-specific representations, provides a promising alternative to conventional one-size-fits-all EEG decoding.

papers.title: An investigation of lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, and work-related outcomes among female teachers: mixed-methods evidence for occupational health promotion.
papers.abstract: Teachers' health and quality of life are important to school health and education policy. This study examined lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, satisfaction, and health-related absence among female schoolteachers in Saudi Arabia. A mixed-methods study in the Eastern Province combined a cross-sectional questionnaire completed by 562 female government-school teachers with semi-structured interviews with 19 teachers. Mental well-being was assessed using the WHO-5. Associations were examined using Spearman correlation and multivariable logistic regression. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive approach. Poor mental well-being (WHO-5 ≤ 50) was reported by 58.4% of teachers, and 24.4% scored ≤28. No moderate-intensity activity was reported by 42.3%; 77.4% of 561 respondents slept six hours or less. Unhealthy foods were consumed several times per week or almost daily by 52.5%; only 29.9% consumed fruit and vegetables daily. Poor or very poor sleep quality was reported by 19.4%, and tobacco use by 3.4%. Overall, 27.9% brushed their teeth less than twice daily, and 52.1% last visited a dentist over two years earlier. Tooth or gum pain at least sometimes during the preceding three months was reported by 61.9%. Sleep quality and duration showed moderate positive correlations with well-being (r = 0.390 and 0.302, respectively; p < 0.001). Physical activity, dietary behaviors, toothbrushing, and oral pain were also associated with well-being. Higher teaching load was weakly associated with lower satisfaction (r = -0.098, p = 0.020). Lifestyle and satisfaction scores remained associated with good well-being after adjustment (OR = 1.051, 95% CI: 1.030-1.073; and 1.035, 95% CI: 1.022-1.048, respectively). Self-rated health also remained associated with good well-being. Lower lifestyle and well-being scores were associated with more health-related absence (all p < 0.05). Five themes described demanding workdays, barriers to healthy routines, emotional strain, work extending into home life, and occupational health concerns. Unhealthy daily routines and poor mental well-being were common among teachers. These findings support greater attention to teacher health in education policy. School health promotion should include manageable work demands, time for rest, and access to preventive care. Sustained investment in workplace health promotion may support teachers' well-being and quality of life.

papers.title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
papers.abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

papers.title: Pathophysiology of REM sleep behaviour disorder.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by loss of muscle atonia and dream enactment behaviour during REM sleep. RBD is recognized as a significant prodromal marker of α-synucleinopathies, but characterizing its unique neuropathological features is challenging due to reliance on individual case reports. Additionally, RBD is not a terminal illness, and data generalisability is limited by the high co-occurrence of α-synucleinopathies. In this review, we discuss the mechanisms responsible for altered REM sleep regulation in RBD, incorporating evidence from human post-mortem histological analyses, structural and functional neuroimaging data on patients with RBD, and pharmacological studies. We explore the risks, biomarkers, and mechanisms of phenoconversion from RBD to α-synucleinopathies, drawing on data from large longitudinal patient cohorts, and we consider disease remission. Lastly, we propose several promising directions for future studies.

papers.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with low back pain among construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia.
papers.abstract: Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability, particularly in labor-intensive industries. While biomechanical hazards are well-documented in developed nations, epidemiological data from unregulated construction sectors in post-conflict regions remains extremely scarce. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and identify factors associated with LBP among manual construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia. An analytic cross-sectional study was conducted among 191 manual workers recruited via stratified random sampling from five major construction companies. Data were collected using a culturally-adapted Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire to assess socio-demographic, lifestyle, and occupational exposures. We utilized a multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression model, accounting for clustering by company, to identify independent associated factors. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The workforce was notably young (median age = 26 years), registering an LBP period prevalence of 51.9% (95% CI: 43.5-60.3%). In the adjusted analysis, income status was the strongest predictor, with workers living below extreme poverty facing elevated odds of LBP (AOR = 7.60; 95% CI: 2.48-23.28). Other factors significantly associated included possessing over six years of work experience (AOR = 4.85; 95% CI: 1.56-15.11), being underweight (AOR = 5.22; 95% CI: 1.24-21.94), tobacco use (AOR = 5.70; 95% CI: 1.94-16.78), and inadequate sleep duration of fewer than six hours (AOR = 4.11; 95% CI: 1.28-13.24). Biomechanically, frequency of heavy lifting (AOR = 4.29; 95% CI: 1.26-14.56) and bending (AOR = 5.35; 95% CI: 1.33-21.45) were strongly associated with reporting LBP. LBP is highly prevalent among construction workers in Mogadishu. The factors associated with LBP were extreme poverty, inadequate physiological tissue recovery, and severe biomechanical overload. Mitigating this crisis requires site-level ergonomic interventions, such as team-lifting protocols, alongside overarching policies that establish baseline wages to address foundational socioeconomic hazards.

papers.title: Psychosocial symptom networks across atrial fibrillation subtypes: evidence from two waves of the ARENA cohort.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) carries substantial psychosocial burden, but how psychosocial symptoms interrelate across AF subtypes and severities remains unclear. This study compared psychosocial symptom networks across time, AF type, and European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA) class in the ARENA (Atrial Fibrillation Rhine-Neckar Region) cohort. Adults with AF were assessed at baseline (T0) and follow-up (T1). Analytic samples included 996 patients with EHRA class [asymptomatic (EHRA 1) vs. symptomatic (EHRA ≥ 2)] and 924 with AF subtype (paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent) data. Measures included anxiety and worry (GAD-2), cardiac worry and avoidance (CAQ-2), health-related quality of life (HRQoL) (EQ-5D-5L), and psychosocial stressors. Gaussian graphical models were estimated and compared using network comparison test. Global network structures were stable across EHRA classes, AF subtypes, and time points, but specific edges and node centralities varied. The most robust edges linked anxiety with general worry and cardiac worry with avoidance. Anxiety, general worry, cardiac worry, and diminished HRQoL were consistently the most central nodes. Among symptomatic (EHRA ≥ 2) patients, loneliness emerged as an increasingly central node over time, whereas among asymptomatic patients (EHRA 1), sleep problems showed a stronger association with HRQoL at follow-up. Atrial fibrillation-type network structures were similar, although paroxysmal networks showed higher node centrality and stronger anxiety-worry coupling at T0; persistent or permanent AF showed a stress-at-home-cardiac worry edge at T1. Psychosocial symptom networks in AF are comparable across subtypes and reveal intervention targets, particularly anxiety, cardiac worry with avoidance, loneliness, and sleep disturbance.

papers.title: The SIK1-NR4A2 axis: a core driver of epilepsy identified by integrated machine learning and experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy remains a major clinical challenge, suggesting that mechanisms beyond the classical excitation-inhibition imbalance contribute to epilepsy. The Liver kinase B1 (LKB1) signaling pathway coordinates energy homeostasis and cell survival, but its key downstream effectors in epilepsy remain largely unknown. We integrated machine learning screening of LKB1 pathway genes using public Gene Expression Omnibus datasets (GSE143272) with in vivo and in vitro experimental validation. A PTZ-induced status epilepticus rat model, AAV-mediated gene knockdown/overexpression, lentiviral transfection of primary hippocampal neurons, Electroencephalography recording, whole-cell patch-clamp recording, and Western blot analysis were employed to investigate the functional role and molecular mechanisms of candidate genes. Machine learning identified SIK1 (salt-inducible kinase 1) as the top-ranked epilepsy risk gene within the LKB1 pathway. SIK1 expression was significantly upregulated in the hippocampus of SE rats. AAV-mediated SIK1 knockdown prolonged seizure latency and reduced seizure duration, while SIK1 overexpression exacerbated seizure severity. Mechanistically, through PPI network analysis and mediation analysis, we identified NR4A2 as a downstream effector of SIK1. SIK1 negatively regulated NR4A2 expression: SIK1 knockdown increased NR4A2, whereas SIK1 overexpression decreased NR4A2. Rescue experiments showed that co-overexpression of SIK1 and NR4A2 reversed the pro-epileptic effect of SIK1 alone. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated that SIK1 knockdown or NR4A2 overexpression restored action potential amplitude to near-normal levels in magnesium-free-treated neurons. SIK1 negatively regulates NR4A2, and restoring NR4A2 expression counteracts SIK1-induced neuronal hyperexcitability. These findings suggest that targeting the SIK1-NR4A2 axis may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for epilepsy.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

papers.title: Heterogeneity and Dynamics of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Rural Boarding Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a global concern in adolescent mental health. Rural boarding middle school students, as a unique and vulnerable population, remain understudied regarding the potential heterogeneity and longitudinal trajectories of NSSI. This study aimed to identify latent classes of NSSI among this group, examine their transition patterns over time, and evaluate the effectiveness of an emotion management group intervention. Study 1 cross-sectionally surveyed 927 adolescents; we split samples into non-NSSI and NSSI subgroups and ran latent profile analysis (LPA) only among participants with NSSI (n=285). Study 2 conducted a 6-month follow-up of 550 participants and applied latent transition analysis (LTA) to examine class shifts and predictive factors. Study 3 was a randomized controlled trial in which 30 students from the High-NSSI received an 8-week emotion-management group intervention. Intervention effects were evaluated using repeated-measures ANCOVA with demographic covariates. Within the NSSI subgroup (n = 285), two classes were identified: a High-NSSI class (n = 21, 7.4%) and a Low-NSSI class (n = 264, 92.6%). Poor sleep quality and bullying victimization independently predicted High-NSSI membership. Longitudinal analysis revealed high stability in the Low-NSSI class (91%) and high fluidity in the High-NSSI class (83% transitioning to low-risk). The emotion-management intervention significantly reduced both NSSI frequency and negative affect. These findings demonstrate that clinically meaningful NSSI subtypes exist among rural boarding adolescents and that sleep quality and bullying are key modifiable risk factors. The results support a stepped-care approach in school settings, where the High-NSSI class requires intensive intervention and the Low-NSSI class may benefit from less intensive, universal supports. The emotion-management group intervention is an effective school-based program for the most severe NSSI subtype.

papers.title: Clinical characteristics, semiology, and comorbidity patterns in non-epileptic seizures (NES): a retrospective comparative study.
papers.abstract: Non-epileptic seizures (NES) are paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures but not explained by ictal activity. Differential diagnosis may be challenging, particularly because NES and epilepsy can coexist. We aimed to characterize the demographic, clinical, semiological, psychiatric, and instrumental profile of patients with NES, compare patients with NES only with patients with NES epilepsy-only, and assess the robustness of the main associations through sensitivity analyses. We conducted a retrospective observational comparative study using a clinical database from our Neurology Unit (2022-2025) including 38 patients with NES and 23 patients with epilepsy without NES. A total of 18 NES patients had comorbid epilepsy; therefore, the primary comparison included mutually exclusive groups: NES-only (n = 20) and epilepsy-only (n = 23). All NES patients were retained for descriptive analyses. Between-group comparisons used exact or non-parametric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) correction. Sensitivity analyses restricted NES-only patients to those with database-recorded video-EEG confirmation and used Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Among 38 patients with NES, 94.7% had documented psychological/psychiatric comorbidity, mainly anxiety (50.0%) and depression (28.9%). Positive motor phenomena were documented in 73.7%, neurological examination inconsistency/incongruity in 85.7% of evaluable patients, and video-EEG confirmation in 73.7%. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was significantly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients (90.0% vs. 13.0%; exact OR 50.40, 95% CI 7.29-670.28; BH-FDR p < 0.001), as was anxiety (45.0% vs. 4.3%; BH-FDR p = 0.014). Broad seizure-semiology domains were not significantly different after multiplicity correction. Among imaged patients, abnormal MRI findings were more frequent in epilepsy-only patients (12/18 vs. 0/10; BH-FDR p = 0.006), although MRI ascertainment differed between groups. The psychiatric-comorbidity association persisted in sensitivity analyses. NES showed substantial clinical heterogeneity and frequently coexisted with epilepsy. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was markedly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients and remained robust in sensitivity analyses, although differential ascertainment limits interpretation. Broad seizure manifestations alone did not distinguish the groups after multiplicity correction. Instrumental findings should be considered descriptive rather than NES biomarkers. These findings support explicit stratification for comorbid epilepsy and standardized prospective assessment of psychiatric and semiological features.

papers.title: Analysis of Motorcycle-involved Crashes in the Philippines from 2010-2019.
papers.abstract: This is a 10-Year retrospective study of motorcycle crashes in the Philippines, which are among the top 9 causes of death in the country. Hence, the need to quantify the severity of motorcycle-involved crashes. The objectives of the study are to determine the epidemiology of motorcycle-involved crashes and to investigate the trend of motorcycle-involved crashes, their proportion against other vehicle types, and how it associates with demographic, clinical, and other hospital and crash variables. Online National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (ONEISS) was used to analyze trends, proportions, and associations for motorcycle-involved crashes. Descriptive and Inferential Statistics were computed to see how motorcycles relate to the other variables for each dataset. Motorcycle crashes comprised the largest percentage from 2010 to 2019, increasing to 6,136 cases and 21,580 cases, respectively. The year 2018 recorded the highest number of motorcycle crash cases with 32,543, which decreased in 2019. The average age of victims of motorcycle-related road crashes is 30.03 years (SD = 14.799). The majority are males (78.2%), single (14.7%), and drivers (65.8%). Linear regression shows that alcohol consumption increases odds for sustaining multiple injuries (OR = 1.826, 95% CI [1.746-1.910]) concussion (OR = 1.158, 95% CI [1.068-1.255]), avulsion (OR = 1.589, 95% CI [1.478-1.708]), and abrasion (OR = 1.545, 95% CI [1.480-1.613]) while being male (OR = 1.552, 95% CI [1.280-1.881]) and lack of sleep (OR = 2.980, 95% CI [1.759-5.047]) increases odds of death among motorcycle-related crash patients. The study showed an increase in motorcycle-related crashes in the Philippines from 2010 to 2019 and the overall impact of motorcycle-involved crashes on drivers and pedestrians. Motorcycles are also the most involved vehicle type in road crashes, and therefore, policies and programs to reduce and prevent motorcycle crashes should be strengthened to prevent motorcycle-related fatalities on the roads.

papers.title: Work-related Road Traffic Injuries in the Philippines: Trends and Determinants from 2010 to 2020.
papers.abstract: Work-related transport and vehicular crashes (TVCs) contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality among the working population and negatively affect economic productivity. Despite the growing burden of road traffic injuries globally, limited data exist on work-related road crashes in the Philippines. The study aimed to describe trends in work-related TVCs in the Philippines from 2010 to 2020 and identify risk factors associated with adverse patient outcomes. Data were obtained from the Department of Health's Online National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (ONEISS) from 2010 to 2020. Cases categorized as work-related under the activity variable were included. Variables analyzed included demographic characteristics, vehicle type, risky road user behaviors, use of safety equipment, and injury type. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize trends. Logistic regression analysis examined factors associated with mortality, while chi-square tests assessed associations between injury patterns and crash-related factors. A total of 15,451 work-related TVC cases were recorded from 2010 to 2020. Reported cases increased from 910 in 2010 to 2,180 in 2019, with a corresponding rise in deaths during the same period. Both cases and deaths declined in 2020, likely due to reduced mobility during the COVID-19 pandemic. Two- and three-wheeled vehicles were the most frequently involved, with motorcycles and tricycles predominating. Alcohol use and sleep-related factors were the most commonly reported risky behaviors. A majority of victims (70.90%) did not practice safe driving behaviors. Significant risk factors for mortality included vehicle type and age, while alcohol use was associated with multiple injuries. Work-related TVCs remain an increasing occupational and public health concern in the Philippines. Strengthening road safety requires coordinated, multi-sectoral action involving government agencies, employers, and workers, with emphasis on road safety education, enforcement of safety measures, and targeted prevention strategies.

papers.title: Restorative streetscapes in high-density urban tourism: environmental archetypes, visual attention, and psychophysiological responses.
papers.abstract: In high-density tourist districts, visitors are continuously exposed to the visual environments of surrounding streets, forecourts, and small public spaces before reaching an attraction, and these transitional spaces may influence short-term restorative states. Existing research has typically examined urban-scale streetscape characteristics and human responses under experimental conditions separately, with limited provision of a reproducible procedure for selecting experimental stimuli from large environmental samples. Taking the high-density urban core around Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour as a case study, this study identified 66 tourism-related sites and acquired four fixed-direction streetscape images for each site, yielding 264 images in total. A 66 × 11 objective environmental matrix was constructed from five GIS-based environmental indicators and six streetscape-image proxy indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarized the dominant environmental gradients, and k = 6 K-means was retained as a pragmatic six-group sampling solution aligned with the pre-specified six-scene experimental capacity rather than as a uniquely optimal or stable urban typology. Forty-six of 48 registered adults contributed 108 focal-scene exposures. After BH-FDR correction, significant differences among the six scenes were observed in perceived restorativeness, the proportion of fixations on natural areas of interest (AOIs), gaze entropy, changes in EEG alpha-minus-theta, mean EDA skin conductance level (SCL), and HRV RMSSD, whereas sustained-attention accuracy showed no significant scene effect. Oil Street Art Space exhibited the highest perceived restorativeness (5.69/7), the highest proportion of fixations on natural AOIs (51.4%), and the largest increases in EEG (+2.68) and HRV RMSSD (+11.37 ms), while Western Market showed the lowest restorativeness (4.17/7), the lowest natural-AOI fixation share (31.2%), and the smallest EEG increase (+1.93). Sensitivity analyses showed no evidence of scene-by-order interaction for perceived restorativeness, natural-AOI fixation, gaze entropy, or SART accuracy, but EEG, EDA, and HRV were more order-sensitive; the principal subjective, attentional, EEG, and HRV contrasts remained evident when analysis was restricted to each participant's earliest focal-scene exposure. These findings therefore support scene-configuration contrasts under short-term static visual exposure. Building on the environmental structure of the 66 sites and the multimodal responses to the six experimental scenes, the study further proposes an archetype-calibrated framework for mapping restorative potential in high-density tourist streetscapes, providing a spatial basis for identifying restorative opportunity nodes and priority intervention areas.

papers.title: Cradle of rebellion: the relationship between bone marrow microenvironment and autoimmune diseases.
papers.abstract: Abnormalities in bone marrow microenvironment (BMM) represent a key mechanism closely related to the occurrence and progression of autoimmune diseases (AIDs). They involve dysfunction of critical microenvironment components: reduced supportive function of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) leads to decreased secretion of the anchoring factor CXCL12, disrupting the quiescent state of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs); dysregulation of sympathetic tone disturbs the circadian rhythm of hematopoietic cell arrangement; and abnormal proliferation of adipocytes fosters a pro-inflammatory environment. Collectively, these changes are related to a functional shift in the microenvironment from homeostasis maintenance to inflammation promotion, directionally biasing HSCs towards differentiation into pro-inflammatory immune lineages and facilitating massive release into the periphery. It establishes a pathogenic vicious cycle: peripheral autoimmune inflammation feeds back to the bone marrow (BM), further remodeling the microenvironment and perpetuating the production of aggressive immune cells, including autoreactive T cells, autoantibody-producing cells, and pro-inflammatory myeloid cells. As a result, patients experience a persistent inflammatory state that resists complete resolution, and disease progression is characterized by systemic involvement, chronicity, and relapsing course. This review focuses on the cellular and molecular components, functional roles, pathological alterations, and mechanisms of the BMM in AIDs. The review aims to provide an essential foundation for further investigation into the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases.

papers.title: A Qualitative Study of Emotional Numbing, Developmental Regression, and the Struggle to Survive Among Gazan Children During Genocide.
papers.abstract: This qualitative study examines the psychological effects of genocide on children in Gaza, with particular attention to emotional numbing, developmental regression, and survival-oriented adaptation under sustained violence. Drawing on in-depth interviews with thirty Palestinian mothers residing in displacement settings in Rafah, Khan Younis, and Nuseirat refugee camp, the analysis identifies six interrelated themes: fear and anxiety associated with airstrikes and drone exposure; nightmares and sleep disruption; emotional dissociation; behavioral dysregulation; apparent acclimatization to ongoing violence; and coping practices grounded in spirituality, creativity, and physical proximity to caregivers. Mothers' accounts illustrate the cumulative nature of psychological distress in a context marked by prolonged displacement and the collapse of institutional, humanitarian, and mental health systems. Patterns of emotional suppression and regression are therefore interpreted not as signs of resilience, but as adaptive responses to extreme and ongoing threat. The study contributes to scholarship on child mental health in contexts of mass violence by highlighting how genocidal conditions reshape trauma expression and limit conventional pathways of recovery, emphasizing the need for trauma-informed approaches that attend to structural and political determinants of children's wellbeing.

papers.title: Sleep in COPD: an understudied and clinically important issue.
papers.abstract: This review provides an overview of objective and subjective sleep characteristics in the general chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) population and discusses associations with airway symptoms, psychological factors, quality of life, and common sleep disorders. Available studies indicate that patients with COPD often exhibit altered sleep architecture, including increased light sleep, reduced slow-wave and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, frequent arousals, reduced sleep efficiency, and shorter total sleep duration. Subjectively, 40-70% of patients report poor sleep quality, characterized by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep and increased daytime sleepiness. Nocturnal respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, wheeze, sputum production, and hypoxemia may contribute to sleep disruption. Common sleep disorders such as insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and restless legs syndrome (RLS) are seen more frequently in COPD, and poor sleep may also negatively affect COPD outcomes through mechanisms such as systemic inflammation, reduced physical activity, and impaired treatment adherence. Sleep disturbances are further associated with anxiety, depression, fatigue, and reduced quality of life. Assessing sleep and sleep quality and treating both COPD and sleep disorders effectively in this patient population are of importance and would likely improve not only sleep and airway symptoms but also quality of life and overall clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Distinct motor preparatory signals correlate with coarse vs fine control of self-paced action timing.
papers.abstract: Making each action at the right time is crucial for motor control. In this study, we investigated how two prominent motor preparatory processes identified in human EEG-beta-band desynchronisation and the readiness potential (RP)-might each differently relate to the time of a simple voluntary action. In our paradigm, participants learned when to act in each block of trials, based on probabilistic trial-by-trial feedback. A reward schedule reinforced a specific optimal time to act in some blocks, but allowed greater variability around the same mean action time in other blocks. We found that contralateral motor beta-band power at the beginning of each trial was higher in trials with slow actions than in those with fast actions. In contrast, contralateral beta-band power reached stereotyped low values at the time of action, regardless of waiting times. Put together, this pattern is consistent with a neural implementation of distance-to-bound for a noisy accumulation process, in which baseline motor activity starts off closer to an action-triggering bound when fast actions are required. In turn, the RP was independent of the mean waiting time before action, but its slope increased when participants developed a precise motor plan. We suggest that beta desynchronisation and the RP track distinct, complementary processes involved in the temporal control of action. While beta-power activity at trial onset is consistent with a strategic adjustment of motor preparation to match the required pace of action, the modulation of the RP by motor plan precision is consistent with a temporally structured input to a ramping preparatory process. Simulations suggest that acting at the right time may involve increasing the strength of the input to this accumulator, which can drive the decision variable to drift towards the decision bound.

papers.title: Different modes of stimulation at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) regulate different EEG microstates under VR immersion conditions.
papers.abstract: Acupuncture at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) alleviates postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nevertheless, the central regulatory effects of PC6 stimulation on virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), a form of physiological vertigo triggered by visual-vestibular sensory conflict, and the corresponding alterations in electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate characteristics remain unclear. Using EEG microstate analysis as the primary approach, this study investigated the effects of different PC6 stimulation modalities on dynamic brain functional changes during VRMS, aiming to further elucidate the potential neural mechanisms underlying acupoint stimulation in VRMS. Participants were recruited based on their Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire scores, with a cut-off value of ≥34 used as the inclusion criterion. A total of 200 healthy participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to four equal groups (n = 50 per group): control (32 °C), 40 °C, 44 °C, and 2-Hz transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS). The experimental protocol consisted of three phases: baseline, active stimulation, and post-stimulation. All participants received a 40-min stimulation targeting the right PC6 acupoint. EEG data were continuously recorded throughout the experiment. Microstate analysis revealed that during the stimulation phase, the 2-Hz TEAS group exhibited significantly increased duration, occurrence, and coverage of microstate D compared with the control group, whereas the 40 °C group affected only the duration of microstate D. During the post-stimulation phase, compared with the control group, the 44 °C group showed a decreased duration of microstate A and significantly increased duration and coverage of microstate B, while the 2-Hz TEAS group continued to exhibit sustained effects on the duration of microstate D. The neuroelectrophysiological signatures of stimulation at PC6 in modulating VRMS are predominantly reflected in the dynamic changes of microstates A, B, and D. Thermal stimulation and low-frequency electrical stimulation engage distinct central modulatory pathways, providing a neuroelectrophysiological basis for optimizing stimulation parameters for in future studies on VRMS.

papers.title: The relationship between the number of chronic conditions and depressive symptoms in older adults with multimorbidity: the chain mediating role of psychological resilience and sleep quality.
papers.abstract: Depression represents a significant global public health challenge for older adults. The relationship between multimorbidity and depressive symptoms has been frequently studied. However, how the number of chronic conditions affects depressive symptoms in older adults with multimorbidity remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the relationship between the number of chronic conditions and depressive symptoms in older adults with multimorbidity, and to investigate the mediating roles of psychological resilience and sleep quality in this relationship. This study utilized cross-sectional survey data collected from two Chinese provinces between October 2024 and January 2025, involving 1,759 older adults with multimorbidity. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 21.0, with Spearman correlation analysis employed to explore associations between key variables. Furthermore, linear regression analysis using Model 6 in the PROCESS 4.2 macro was conducted to assess the relationship between the number of chronic conditions and depressive symptoms and to examine the chain-mediating effects of psychological resilience and sleep quality in this relationship. Among older adults with multimorbidity, the number of chronic conditions was significantly associated with depressive symptoms (β = 0.094, 95% CI: 0.059, 0.130). Psychological resilience (β = 0.064, 95% CI: 0.042, 0.086) and sleep quality (β = 0.044, 95% CI: 0.030, 0.060) each mediated the relationship between the number of chronic conditions and depressive symptoms, accounting for 30.05 and 20.66% of the total effect, respectively. Additionally, a chain-mediating effect involving both psychological resilience and sleep quality was observed (β = 0.011, 95% CI: 0.007, 0.015), contributing 5.16% to the total effect. This study found that psychological resilience and sleep quality mediated the association between the number of chronic conditions and depressive symptoms in older adults with multimorbidity. In health management practice, greater attention could be given to the assessment of psychological resilience and sleep quality, together with psychological support and sleep health management, to support the comprehensive management of depressive symptoms. Due to the cross-sectional design, causal direction and temporal ordering cannot be inferred.

papers.title: CEP-MI: a novel cue-execution dual-stage motor imagery paradigm with PGCANet decoding architecture.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) holds great potential in neurorehabilitation and motor assistance. Data quality and motor intention decoding effectiveness are closely associated with participants' engagement. However, previous MI tasks ignored active engagement regulation, and neural mechanisms underlying the transition from motor imagery to execution remain unclear, with limited relevant research. Conventional separate-trial designs cannot capture continuous brain dynamics from imagery to execution and cannot objectively evaluate subject engagement, which hinders mechanism exploration and stable decoding. To address these paradigm-related limitations, a novel cue-execution MI paradigm (CEP-MI) with countdown anchors was designed to quantify engagement. Motor execution sessions were added post-imagery to reveal neural differences during the transition and identify movement-related brain activities. Meanwhile, to boost MI-EEG decoding performance, a collaborative decoding architecture (PGCANet) integrating prior guidance and channel awareness was proposed, with dual branches and consistency constraint loss for decision fusion. CEP-MI effectively quantifies participant engagement, and PGCANet achieves superior decoding performance compared to traditional algorithms and advanced models, with the optimal average accuracy reaching 85.77% in binary classification and 82.47% in quadruple classification. Targeting the above-mentioned research gaps, the CEP-MI paradigm provides valuable insights into the imagery-execution transition mechanism. PGCANet enhances MI decoding accuracy via multi-branch collaboration, laying a foundation for MI-BCI's clinical application in neurorehabilitation. This study introduces a novel paradigm and collaborative architecture that significantly advance MI-BCI decoding accuracy and engagement quantification, and helps to promote its clinical application in neurorehabilitation.

papers.title: Modifiable risk factors for mild cognitive impairment: Insights from a 7-year follow-up cohort study among Shanghai community-dwelling older adults.
papers.abstract: We aimed to identify key modifiable risk factors (MRFs) for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) among community-dwelling older adults in Shanghai by incorporating potential China-specific factors into established MRF frameworks at an earlier stage of Alzheimer's disease. Baseline cognitively normal participants from the Shanghai Brain Aging Study (N = 2464) were selected and followed for a maximum of 7 years, with demographic, lifestyle, and clinical data and comprehensive neuropsychological assessments. Cox regression and population attributable fraction (PAF) were used to quantify the contribution of MRFs to incident MCI. Sex stratification analyses were used for exploratory purposes. At follow-up, 26.7% of individuals had developed MCI. Six MRFs were included in the PAF analysis. Somatic comorbidity (diabetes or cerebral infarction, hazard ratio [HR] = 1.84), manual labor (HR = 1.47), short sleep duration (HR = 1.45), and lack of soy products (HR = 1.36) were the principal contributors. Divorced or widowed status and persistent depressive mood contributed weakly and non-significantly. Together, these six MRFs accounted for a PAF of 19.22% after adjustment for age and education. The overall PAF was higher in females (22.94%) than in males (13.10%), with a broader range of contributing factors in females. Six MRFs accounted for nearly 20% of MCI at the population level in this 7-year follow-up Shanghai community population, extending the modifiable-risk framework from dementia to its earlier prodromal stage and providing novel insights for early dementia prevention.

papers.title: Sleep components, depressive subdomains and quality of life in Parkinson's disease: A cross-sectional exploratory analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms are prevalent non-motor burdens in Parkinson's disease (PD) and are closely associated with poorer health-related quality of life (QoL). Non-motor symptoms of PD exhibit substantial heterogeneity. It remains unclear whether distinct sleep disturbances show differential correlations with physical and mental QoL, and whether specific depressive subdimensions are implicated in these relationships. This exploratory study analyzed direct and indirect associations among sleep components, depressive subdimensions, and physical-mental QoL in hospitalized patients with PD. This retrospective study analyzed data from 55 hospitalized patients with idiopathic PD who completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). Spearman correlation and multivariable regression analyses were performed to assess bivariate associations and independent correlates of QoL. Exploratory PROCESS analyses were further implemented as hypothesis-generating secondary analyses to examine symptom-level indirect associations; all findings were interpreted as cross-sectional and non-causal. Spearman correlation analyses showed that the PSQI total score was significantly correlated with both PCS and MCS (both p < 0.01). Multivariable regression demonstrated that the HAMD total score was the only significant independent correlate of PCS (p = 0.025) and MCS (p = 0.004), whereas the PSQI total score reached no statistical significance in either model (p = 0.424 and p = 0.617, respectively). Exploratory PROCESS analyses identified two distinct symptom-level indirect association patterns: nocturnal sleep disturbances correlated with reduced physical QoL through HAMD Retardation, and poor subjective sleep quality correlated with lower mental QoL through HAMD Anxiety/Somatization. Within this hospitalized PD cohort, depressive symptoms represented the dominant correlate of QoL. Specific sleep components exhibited indirect association patterns with QoL through distinct depressive subdimensions. These preliminary findings underline the heterogeneity of PD non-motor symptoms and provide a hypothesis-generating framework for future longitudinal validation and targeted intervention studies.

papers.title: Cardiovascular health and longevity: where are we?
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular health is a key factor in human longevity, affecting not just lifespan but also the quality of aging. We synthesize evidence across four risk factor domains: genetic and epigenetic factors (APOE, FOXO3, telomere biology, epigenetic clocks); metabolic and vascular factors (hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, obesity, arterial stiffness); lifestyle determinants (diet, physical activity, smoking, sleep, gut microbiome); and environmental exposure (air and noise pollution, climate stressors, ionizing radiation). These factors influence various biological processes such as oxidative stress, chronic low grade inflammation (inflammaging), mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic disturbances, and changes in telomere length and epigenetics that collectively damage the endothelium, stiffen arteries, promote atherosclerosis, and contribute to overall cardiovascular decline with age. Understanding these processes helps explain why cardiovascular aging is such a strong predictor of mortality. We further summarize the principal intervention strategies with evidence for improving cardiovascular health and longevity, such as adherence to the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 construct, heart-healthy dietary patterns(Mediterranean, DASH), smoking cessation, sleep optimization, and reduction of environmental exposures. This narrative review distinguishes evidence derived from model organisms, human observational cohorts, and human interventional/genetic studies, since these evidence tiers differ substantially in their support for lifespan or longevity extending claims specifically, as opposed to cardiovascular risk reduction more broadly.

papers.title: Predictors of Psychological Stress and Infertility Among Reproductive-Age Women in Jammu and Kashmir: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Infertility affects nearly one in six individuals globally, with a substantial proportion of cases remaining idiopathic. Emerging evidence suggests that psychological stress may influence reproductive outcomes through neuroendocrine and immune pathways, potentially influencing the vaginal microbiome and the reproductive microenvironment. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of stress and infertility and examine their association among women of reproductive age in Jammu and Kashmir. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 1068 married women aged 18-48 years in Jammu and Kashmir, including women with idiopathic infertility and fertile controls. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, perceived stress, symptoms of reproductive tract infections (RTIs), sleep patterns, and physical stress manifestations were collected using a structured interviewer-administered questionnaire. Binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with psychological stress and infertility. Overall, 37.6% of participants reported stress, while 29.3% had infertility. Stress was significantly associated with older age groups, employment status, lower financial status, RTI symptoms, physical stress manifestations, sleep duration, and infertility. Women with infertility had markedly higher odds of stress. Infertility was significantly associated with a history of stress, age, employment status, financial status, RTI symptoms, and sleep duration. Psychological stress is strongly associated with infertility and related health and socioeconomic factors among women in this population. These findings highlight the potential interplay between psychological, reproductive, and social factors in reproductive health. Further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and inform targeted interventions.
